content: The Boysproject is a social organization based in Antwerp, Belgium, that supports male and transgender sex workers. It utilizes social media to raise awareness about social and medical services, provide information, and facilitate referrals. The organization’s website includes resources and chat boxes where individuals can ask questions and receive guidance on sexual health and related issues. Additionally, Boysproject operates a drop-in center every Wednesday afternoon, which is promoted online and via SMS. This center offers services from a social worker and a doctor, a Dutch language course, and a space for conversation, sharing experiences, and enjoying food. Social workers play a critical role in educating individuals about PEP and supporting them through the process. In 2013, Boysproject reached 298 sex workers, including 165 new contacts, an increase from 229 (140 new contacts) in 2012. Approximately 1,130 invitations to the drop-in center were sent via social media in 2013, with 15–30 sex workers attending weekly. The PASMO/PSI Combination Prevention Program aims to improve access to HIV prevention interventions for key populations in six Central American countries. The program focuses on reducing high-risk behaviors, addressing social hostility such as homophobia and stigma, increasing access to essential prevention and health services, and strengthening research and monitoring. It provides a comprehensive package of behavioral, biomedical, and structural interventions tailored to each target population. Services include behavior change communication, STI screening and treatment, medical care referrals, and support for issues like family planning, stigma, legal aid, and substance abuse treatment. AFEW (AIDS Foundation East-West) operates in several countries, including Georgia, Kazakhstan, and Ukraine, to reduce the impact of HIV on key populations. Through client management initiatives, AFEW strengthens the capacity of local governments, NGOs, and community providers while coordinating service networks. Client management involves collaboration between individuals, client managers, and service providers to improve timely access to health and psychosocial care. Social workers and client managers, often from key population communities, are trained in human rights, ethics, and new approaches to working with target groups. AFEW also organizes workshops and events to share experiences and best practices, fostering improved service integration and collaboration. The Egyptian Family Planning Association (EFPA) extends its clinical services through outreach to engage young people at high risk of HIV. Volunteer peer educators, aged 18–25, provide comprehensive, gender-sensitive, rights-based sexual and reproductive health education. Outreach sessions target young people under 18, including street children and orphans, in non-clinical settings to maintain confidentiality. Educators explain clinic services, encourage attendance, and distribute condoms. In 2012, EFPA conducted 81 peer-to-peer sessions, reaching nearly 2,300 individuals, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and young people who inject drugs. EFPA also advocates for policy changes to prioritize young people's sexual and reproductive health needs within the national health system. The Pehchan program in India strengthens the capacity of 200 community-based organizations (CBOs) to deliver HIV prevention services to over 450,000 MSM, transgender individuals, and hijras. The program complements the government’s HIV prevention strategy by providing additional services that foster an enabling environment for healthy behaviors. Pehchan emphasizes community ownership, with members of key populations serving as program managers and advisors. The program has developed crisis response teams to address violence and initiated a national advocacy campaign to decriminalize homosexuality. Efforts also focus on reducing HIV stigma within key populations through outreach and counseling. LVCT Health in Kenya provides essential services to MSM and sex workers outside traditional settings to overcome barriers to care. Peer-led interventions involve community members at all stages of the program. Hotspots are mapped with community leaders, and services include HIV testing, STI screening, and cervical cancer screening for female sex workers. Clients diagnosed with HIV are linked to treatment and care, with over 85% retention in care and 90% adherence to treatment. LVCT Health’s advocacy has influenced Kenya’s National HIV Strategic Plan, paving the way for national-scale service delivery for key populations. The National Organization of Peer Educators (NOPE) in Kenya developed the Drop-In Service Centre (DiSC) model to provide one-stop HIV services for female sex workers and MSM. DiSCs are strategically located in hotspots and offer services such as STI treatment, psychosocial support, and harm reduction education. Peer educators, often from key populations, are trained to manage DiSCs. NOPE has served 20,000 individuals and contributed to national guidelines for key populations. The model emphasizes trust-building and integration of services into national health systems for sustainability. The Marsa Sexual Health Centre in Beirut provides sexual and reproductive health services in a stigma-free environment, targeting marginalized communities, including MSM and transgender individuals. Outreach is conducted through social media and word-of-mouth, encouraging individuals to access services without fear of discrimination. Médecins du Monde (MdM) in Myanmar offers comprehensive STI and HIV prevention, treatment, and harm reduction services for sex workers, MSM, and people who use drugs. Services are provided free of charge at drop-in centers and clinics. MdM emphasizes addressing basic health needs alongside harm reduction to strengthen program acceptance and reduce misunderstandings. The Naz Male Health Alliance (NMHA) in Pakistan addresses the health and psychosocial needs of MSM and transgender individuals through six service delivery centers. These centers provide a safe space and are staffed primarily by community members. NMHA has significantly increased HIV diagnoses among MSM and transgender individuals in public treatment centers. The organization collaborates with national and international stakeholders to enhance service delivery and advocacy. Save the Children in Thailand uses information and communication technologies (ICT) to enhance HIV prevention outreach to MSM and transgender individuals. Social media platforms and mobile apps are used to engage these populations, providing information on HIV prevention and care. Outreach workers use tablets to facilitate communication and establish trust with clients, ensuring continued online contact and support. Kimara Peers in Tanzania operates drop-in centers near state-run health facilities to serve young people who use drugs and sell sex. Services include psychosocial therapy, harm reduction education, and referrals for STI treatment. The program maintains confidentiality and seeks government approval for clean needle distribution.
